content: Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP) can result in airway obstruction. There are two primary patterns of RRP: juvenile-onset RRP (JoRRP) and adult-onset RRP. In JoRRP, the virus is transmitted from mother to child during birth, with symptoms typically appearing in children aged 1 to 4 years. Adult-onset RRP is believed to be sexually acquired, potentially through oro-genital contact or from a latent HPV infection acquired earlier in life. The introduction of prophylactic vaccines targeting HPV types 6 and 11 has significantly reduced the incidence of JoRRP and genital warts. The diagnosis of genital warts is made by identifying flat, papular, or pedunculated growths on the anogenital skin or mucosa during a medical examination. HPV-related cancers may present with abnormal bleeding, discharge, or non-healing lesions or ulcers. Since HPV cannot be cultured using conventional methods, molecular testing is employed for both epidemiological surveillance and clinical applications. Epidemiological testing requires type-specific assays with high analytical sensitivity, while clinical testing serves as a marker for underlying or incipient disease. Self-collected genital samples have been shown to be as effective as clinician-collected cervical samples for molecular testing. Screening for low-risk HPV types is not clinically indicated, as cancer precursors are associated only with high-risk HPV types. Prophylactic HPV vaccines, developed using viral-like particles (VLPs) that mimic the infectious virus, have proven to be highly immunogenic and effective. These vaccines elicit high-titer, type-specific, neutralizing antibodies and have demonstrated safety and efficacy in preventing HPV-related infections and diseases, including cervical precancerous lesions and neoplasia, in phase 3 clinical trials. Protection and immunogenicity last for at least 12–15 years, with ongoing monitoring of the duration of protection. Vaccines are most effective when administered before sexual debut but also provide benefits to adults, including protection against infection, genital warts, and anal canal disease. Cervical screening, traditionally performed using the Papanicolaou (Pap) smear and more recently with liquid-based cytology, has been a cornerstone of cervical cancer prevention. Screening every 2–3 years is effective when supported by robust sampling systems, sample transport, and assessment by experienced pathologists. High-quality assurance and control, along with appropriate follow-up and treatment of precancerous lesions, are essential for the success of cervical screening. HPV testing offers better specificity and a high negative predictive value, allowing women who test negative to be retested after a minimum interval of five years. The effectiveness of HPV screening for preventing anal and oropharyngeal cancers is under evaluation. For the treatment of external, uncomplicated anogenital warts caused by HPV, various options are available for adults, adolescents, pregnant women, and people living with HIV. Treatment recommendations are based on evidence from high-quality meta-analyses, systematic reviews, and randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Complete lesion response rates vary depending on the treatment modality, with electrosurgery/electrocautery showing the highest response rates and podophyllin 20% showing the lowest. Adverse effects such as erythema, edema, itching, watery discharge, and initial pain are associated with some treatments but typically resolve within days to a week. Creams and solutions are often preferred due to their feasibility and acceptability, though costs and availability vary by country and setting. Cryotherapy is considered the safest option during pregnancy. The choice of treatment should consider factors such as the size, thickness, and anatomical location of the warts. Close monitoring is essential, especially when using less effective treatments like podophyllin resin, which may be an alternative when other options are unavailable. Podophyllotoxin solution or cream, imiquimod cream, trichloroacetic acid, and podophyllin resin are contraindicated during pregnancy. Guidelines for the treatment of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including anogenital warts, are based on the best available evidence. However, the epidemiology and patterns of antimicrobial resistance vary geographically and require ongoing monitoring. In areas lacking local data, the global recommendations can be adopted as they have been assessed for applicability across diverse settings. Local availability of medicines and the competencies of health workers should also be considered. Quantifying medicine needs is critical for estimating costs and ensuring an adequate supply. This involves reviewing medicine unit prices, quantities required per treatment, and epidemiological data on infection prevalence. Medicines can be procured through international vendors, generic product suppliers, and non-profit organizations to minimize costs. Joint procurement schemes between countries can further reduce costs by sharing overhead expenses and leveraging bulk discounts. Including STI medicines on national essential medicine lists increases the likelihood of achieving a low-cost supply. Efforts to adapt and implement STI guidelines should promote and protect the human rights of individuals requiring care, ensuring that stigma and discrimination are prevented. Gender equity and voluntary use of services should be emphasized. Key populations disproportionately affected by STIs, including people living with HIV, should have increased access to STI services and treatment. WHO’s 2022 Consolidated Guidelines on HIV, viral hepatitis, and STI prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations provide additional recommendations and guidance. Early and effective treatment of STIs requires promoting healthcare-seeking behavior, providing high-quality care, offering immediate treatment, and ensuring partner notification and treatment services. Screening for STIs in high-risk populations and strengthening case-finding efforts are also essential. Laboratory or point-of-care diagnostics should be available for the detection and management of STIs. For trichomoniasis, evidence on the effects of tinidazole, secnidazole, and ornidazole is limited, necessitating further RCTs to compare these medicines with multiple doses of metronidazole. For Mycoplasma genitalium, global epidemiological surveillance is needed to monitor prevalence and antimicrobial resistance. RCTs are required to compare alternative regimens to moxifloxacin and evaluate sequential therapies. The development of new antimicrobial agents for M. genitalium is also necessary. For bacterial vaginosis, RCTs are needed to compare tinidazole with metronidazole and to study approaches for managing recurrent cases. For anogenital warts, outcomes such as quality of life, patient preferences, and cost-effectiveness should be assessed. Additional research is needed for people living with HIV and other immunocompromised groups. Consideration should also be given to the risk of airborne HPV dispersal in healthcare workers performing ablations. WHO will work with regional and national partners to adapt, implement, and monitor these guidelines. Dissemination will occur through conferences, electronic media, and integration into WHO’s forthcoming Consolidated Guidelines for STI prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care. A system for monitoring new evidence and updating recommendations will be established, ensuring consistency across WHO products.
